profiles.meeting_scenario: At a university hospital electrophysiology research unit, a cardiac electrophysiologist and a clinical epidemiologist are holding a design review of a near-final evidence extraction framework and analysis plan for an updated systematic review/meta-analysis comparing time-to-isolation-based cryoballoon protocols with conventional cryoballoon protocols for atrial fibrillation ablation. The draft extends the published review beyond June 2020 and is intended for PROSPERO registration and journal submission. The agenda is to check whether the current extraction sheet, endpoint tables, and subgroup rules are 'submission-ready,' especially for efficacy at 1 year, safety reporting, device-generation subgrouping, and the real-time pulmonary vein potential recording outcome. The expected outcome is a go/no-go decision on the current design with minor revisions assigned, without reopening the whole project.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.role: Cardiac Electrophysiologist and Clinical Lead Reviewer
members.expertise: Atrial fibrillation ablation, cryoballoon workflows, interpretation of electrophysiology trial endpoints
members.background: Dr. Park directs the hospital's AF ablation program and has participated in device evaluation studies involving second-generation cryoballoon systems. She reviews manuscripts primarily from the standpoint of clinical comparability across ablation protocols.
members.private_state: She wants the review to be clinically credible to electrophysiologists and is wary of methodological choices that mix unlike procedural contexts, because she expects peer reviewers to challenge any synthesis that does not respect practical differences in how cryoballoon cases are run.
hidden_assumptions: When a paper reports a '1-year' arrhythmia outcome, the clinically valid version is recurrence status after the standard 90-day blanking period and assessed close to 12 months post-index ablation, not just any follow-up nearest that time.

References to 'second-generation cryoballoon' in this topic should be limited to the original Arctic Front Advance platform, because newer variants and mixed-platform cohorts can subtly change mapping and procedural behavior.

A 'complication' table in an ablation meta-analysis should capture periprocedural or early post-procedure safety events tied directly to the index ablation, not broader downstream events during long-term follow-up.
The 'real-time recording rate' is meaningful only when calculated at the pulmonary-vein level, because time-to-isolation is determined vein by vein rather than patient by patient.

members.name: Dr. Omar Singh
members.expertise: Systematic reviews, meta-analysis methods, outcome harmonization across heterogeneous cardiovascular studies
members.background: Dr. Singh supports cardiovascular evidence syntheses for multiple departments and has led protocol development for comparative effectiveness reviews involving mixed study designs and inconsistent endpoint reporting.
members.private_state: He wants the review design to remain inclusive enough to preserve statistical power and reduce selective exclusion, because he is concerned that overly narrow harmonization rules will leave too few studies for pooled estimates and subgroup analysis.
hidden_assumptions: A '1-year' efficacy endpoint can be operationalized as the reported rhythm outcome closest to 12 months, even if studies differ in blanking-period handling or report windows such as 9-15 or 12-18 months.
For subgrouping, 'second-generation cryoballoon' is a family label that reasonably includes Advance Pro and mixed cohorts dominated by second-generation use unless a study is clearly incompatible.
If authors label something as a procedure-related adverse event or complication anywhere in follow-up, it belongs in the pooled safety frame unless it is obviously unrelated to the ablation.

For extraction consistency, the 'real-time recording rate' is adequately represented at the patient or procedure level when papers report the proportion of cases with successful real-time signal capture, since many studies do not provide vein-level denominators.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 1-year efficacy endpoint
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say they will use the '1-year freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia' endpoint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means recurrence-free status after the blanking period, measured at approximately 12 months after the index ablation, with preference for studies whose endpoint is explicitly framed that way.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means whichever arrhythmia-free outcome is reported closest to 12 months, even if the paper uses a different blanking convention or a wider follow-up window.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because '1-year freedom from ATs' is standard language in AF ablation papers, both assume the phrase already anchors a common definition; the divergence sits in the silently accepted harmonization rule rather than the named outcome itself.

misalignment_points.topic: Which studies belong in the second-generation cryoballoon subgroup
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to reviewing the 'second-generation balloon subgroup.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking specifically of studies using the original Arctic Front Advance system and would treat Advance Pro or mixed-platform cohorts as meaningfully different unless separately extractable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the broader class of second-generation cryoballoon studies, including Advance Pro and cohorts where second-generation systems predominate.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In everyday EP discussion, 'second-generation balloon' is often used as shorthand without repeating exact model names, so the phrase feels precise enough even though each person maps it to a different set of studies.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the pooled safety analysis
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about keeping a single 'complications' table for safety.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the table covers periprocedural and early post-ablation complications such as phrenic nerve palsy, tamponade, vascular injury, and early stroke/TIA, typically through discharge or 30 days.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the table can include any study-reported procedure-related adverse events across follow-up, including late pulmonary vein stenosis or arrhythmia-related rehospitalization if authors categorize them under complications.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A single safety table is normal in a review, and many papers themselves compress early and later adverse events under broad labels; since both want comprehensive safety reporting, neither feels the need to restate the time boundary.

misalignment_points.topic: Denominator for real-time pulmonary vein potential recording
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the extraction sheet should capture the 'real-time recording rate.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the proportion of pulmonary veins in which real-time potential recording was obtained, because that reflects whether TTI could actually be observed vein by vein.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the proportion of patients or procedures in which any real-time recording was achieved, because that is the most commonly extractable form across heterogeneous reports.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'recording rate' sounds self-explanatory and is reported inconsistently across papers; both assume the other is using the obvious denominator, so the false consensus survives a normal review conversation.

turns.inner_thought: We're close, but I don't want this to go out with sloppy clinical grouping that an EP reviewer will immediately pick apart. If we keep efficacy anchored to the usual post-blanking 12-month rhythm outcome, keep the original second-generation cryoballoon cases together, and keep safety focused on true index-procedure complications, this will read as clinically serious rather than methodologically convenient.

turns.inner_thought: The design is basically set. My main concern is avoiding late-stage narrowing that forces us to re-screen or discard usable studies, because the updated literature is heterogeneous enough already. If Lena signs off on the harmonization rules as drafted, we can keep the review inclusive and preserve enough studies for pooled estimates and subgroup work.

turns.inner_thought: The efficacy line is the biggest place where people can quietly mix unlike outcomes. When I say 1-year freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia, I mean the standard clinical endpoint after the 90-day blanking period and assessed around 12 months after index ablation. If papers drift too far from that framing, reviewers will say we're combining different efficacy constructs.

The plan is already to take whatever rhythm outcome each paper reports nearest to 12 months so we don't throw away newer studies with broader visit windows or slightly different blanking conventions. turns.utterance: Yes, and that's how the worksheet is set up now. We'll use the rhythm outcome nearest 12 months from each paper, which should let us preserve the 1-year freedom from atrial tachyarrhythmia pool across the updated set.

turns.inner_thought: Next issue: device generation. turns.utterance: The other area I want to keep tight is subgrouping. In particular, I want the second-generation balloon subgroup to stay clean, because a lot of the clinical interpretation hinges on how people think those cases were actually done.

turns.inner_thought: Safety doesn't need to become sprawling. One complications table should cover the key periprocedural and early post-ablation events tied to the index procedure—phrenic nerve palsy, tamponade, vascular issues, early neurologic events. If we keep it focused and add a dedicated phrenic nerve palsy row, reviewers will get what they need quickly.
turns.utterance: On safety, I actually think the manuscript is nicely concise. One pooled complications table, plus a dedicated phrenic nerve palsy row, should be enough for most reviewers if we keep the presentation straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed. A single safety frame is cleaner, and I'd rather absorb all study-labeled procedure-related adverse events into that same table than create arbitrary splits by timing that many papers don't report consistently. If something is presented by authors as a complication related to the procedure, it belongs in the pooled safety picture unless it's clearly unrelated.
turns.utterance: I agree. And from the analysis side, that same complications table can absorb the procedure-related adverse events authors report later in follow-up as well, so the safety narrative stays unified instead of fragmenting across sections.

turns.inner_thought: Last check: the real-time recording rate needs to stay in the extraction sheet because it helps show whether the TTI-guided approach was truly individualized at the pulmonary vein level. If that field drops out, we lose an important mechanistic read on whether time-to-isolation could actually be observed where it mattered.
